description: Spain conquered with soldiers but ruled with workers: the encomienda grant, demographic collapse, the turn to enslaved African labor, and the casta order built on top.
essential_question: Who did the work of empire, and why did the answer change?

key_terms.definition: A Spanish labor grant giving a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from Indigenous communities, justified as protection and Christian instruction.
The rapid, massive decline of Indigenous populations after contact, driven chiefly by Afro-Eurasian diseases to which they had no immunity.
The forced transport of enslaved Africans to the Americas to supply the colonial labor that Indigenous workers could no longer provide.
The colonial hierarchy ranking people by ancestry, from peninsulares and criollos at the top to Indians and Africans at the bottom.

learning_objectives: Describe how the encomienda system granted and justified claims to Indigenous labor.
Explain how disease and overwork produced a labor shortage in the Spanish colonies.
Trace the economic logic that connected the dying Indigenous workforce to the transatlantic slave trade.
Describe the casta hierarchy and how it ordered colonial society by ancestry.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [solemn]When Columbus reached the island of Hispaniola, more than a million Taíno people farmed, fished, and raised families there. Within decades, by one Spanish count, only a few hundred were left. [beat] Conquest is a story about soldiers. But empire is a story about workers. Silver had to be mined. Sugar had to be cut. And the Spanish Empire ran on one question: who would do the work?

narration.text: Protection and Christianity. That was the deal. [beat] The practice was different. The [es]encomenderos[/es] ruled like feudal lords. They worked whole villages to death in the mines and the fields, and sent the Crown its cut of the silver. [beat] A friar named Bartolomé de Las Casas saw it and wrote it down. His book, written in [date:1542], shocked Spain. The Crown answered with the [es]repartimiento[/es] reforms of [date:1549]. No more private grants. The Crown would assign the labor directly. [beat] The treatment did not improve. But the control did.

narration.text: [solemn]And then the workers started dying. Smallpox, influenza, measles. Diseases no one on these continents had ever met. Between 1500 and 1650, somewhere between half and nine in ten Native people in the Americas died. On Hispaniola, overwork finished what disease started. [beat] Las Casas walked through the ruins and wrote what he saw.

beats.cue: the children of slaves were slaves
engine of the new labor system

narration.text: Spain turned to enslaved African labor, bought through the trade the Portuguese had already built to feed Europe's sugar islands. They carried greater resistance to Old World diseases, and the Spanish saw them as replaceable through the trade, torn from their homelands and easier to control. [beat] And here the story takes a darker turn. Slavery was ancient. But starting in the 1500s, it changed. Now it was for life. Now the children of slaves were slaves. Now a human being was property, with no rights at all. [beat] That idea, that a person could be owned the way you own a tool, became the engine of the new labor system. And it would outlive the Spanish Empire by centuries.

effects.cue: And your place decided your work

beats.cue: And your place decided your work

narration.text: On top of the labor system, Spain built a social order to match. [beat] Look at this painting. A Mexican artist, in [date:1763], painted the colony the way it saw itself. What is it telling you? [2s pause] It is a ladder. At the top, [es]peninsulares[/es], born in Spain, and [es]criollos[/es], Spaniards born in the Americas. One or two in a hundred people. Below them, [es]mestizos[/es], then [es]mulatos[/es]. At the bottom, Indians and Africans. [beat] The Spanish called it the [es]sistema de castas[/es]. It was rooted in an old Spanish obsession, [es]limpieza de sangre[/es], purity of blood. Your ancestors decided your place. And your place decided your work. [beat] In theory rigid. In practice, people moved, mixed, and bought their way up.

scenes.production_notes: Show-and-ask: open on a tight crop of two figures only, ask the question aloud, hold the full 2s pause, then pull back to the full painting on 'It is a ladder.' Then the annotated freeze-frame: the ladder list draws on beside the figures with ink circles marking each named group. Coordinates must be tuned against the actual panel at animatic stage. The stamped verdict (THE CASTA LADDER) doubles as the LO4 ✓. Silence under the pause; single low thud under the stamp.
